newsitem.title: UK: Small Europe refiners feed on oil majors' scraps.
newsitem.headline: Small Europe refiners feed on oil majors' scraps.

text.p: A small Dutch company is blazing a trail in the European oil refining industry where its bigger multinational rivals fear to tread.
Petroplus International said on Monday it had reached agreement with Daewoo to buy the South Korean company's 65,000 barrels per day (bpd) Antwerp refinery.
The move comes against a background of downsizing, mergers and price wars between the oil giants which are still struggling to sell refineries in France and Britain.
Analysts say the trend to shed refining capacity may be bottoming out and some see a trend towards more adaptable oil companies that can react quickly to the changing downstream environment.

"Tosco have been leading the way in the United States, but we also see a role in Europe for a tightly focussed and agile downstream company," said Marcel Van Poecke, managing partner at Petroplus International.
In just a few meteoric years, Tosco Petroleum has risen to become the largest independent refiner in the United States.
Lauded by Wall Street as a model of efficiency for larger oil companies, it now has a refining capacity similar to integrated majors Exxon and Mobil.
Other oil trading outfits have also been quick to selectively snap up downstream assets in recent years.
Vitol SA is perhaps the most successful trading house to emerge from a devastating oil market shakeout in the late 1980s.
The Swiss-based trading house bought the 105,000 bpd Come-by-Chance refinery in Canada and has tended to buy only those downstream assets that complement its core trading expertise.
Earlier this year Louis Dreyfus, a privately owned French trader, finally gained full control of the 180,000 bpd Wilhelmshaven plant in northern Germany.
The refinery is one of the lowest cost units in Europe and relies on a highly skilled team of traders to make it profitable.
Van Poecke sees smaller companies evolving as oil giants continue to shed downstream assets that do not fit their leaner view of the future.
But he is keen to echo the cautious approach of Vitol and Dreyfus.
"What we are aiming to do is complement rather than compete with the major oil companies," he said.

Petroplus already has storage facilities in Germany, Denmark and in the Rotterdam area as well as experience of crude processing at refineries in Belarus and Lithuania through its subsidiary Marimpex.
"We feel comfortable operating with the storage facilities that we have and can respond quickly to the changing environmental legislation," said Van Poecke.
He said Petroplus would bring back on stream units at the refinery which have recently been mothballed -- a reformer and a de-sulphurisation unit.
"We aim to operate it as an independent low cost refinery," he added.
Van Poecke declined to say how much the refinery cost but other industry sources suggested a figure around $10 million.
The much larger Wilhelmshaven refinery bought by Dreyfus went for about $60 million, industry sources said.
Meanwhile, Chevron Corp and British Petroleum Co Plc are still trying to sell refineries in Wales and France respectively.
BP says that it has rejected a number of offers for its refinery in Lavera but that the plant remains for sale.
Rolf Stomberg, head of refining and market at BP, said in June that the equivalent of six European refineries needed to close in order to balance the continent's oil products market.
But Mehdi Varzi, analyst at Kleinwort Benson Securities, sees a much tighter market than that.
"That's too bearish," he said. Growing world demand and increased U.S. imports were helping soak up the European surplus, he added.
